build('landau_g', "Landau's $g(n)$ from a Complete Partition Search", r"""
\begin{abstract}
The order of a permutation is the least common multiple of its cycle lengths, so
Landau's function $g(n)$ --- the largest order of an element of the symmetric
group $S_n$ --- is the largest lcm taken over the partitions of $n$. Computing it
is therefore a search, and a search returns a theorem about all cycle types only
if the enumeration it walks is known to be complete.

We give a fuelled generator for the non-increasing partitions, prove both that
everything it produces is a partition of $n$ and that every partition of $n$ is
produced, and read $g(n)$ off it for $n \le 10$. The values are
$1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 6, 12, 15, 20, 30$. The first departure from intuition is at
$n = 7$, where the maximum is carried by the cycle type $4 + 3$ rather than by
the $7$-cycle: coprimality buys more than length.
\end{abstract}

\section{The quantity}

A permutation of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ decomposes into disjoint cycles whose lengths
form a partition of $n$, and its order is the lcm of those lengths. Hence
\[
  \boxed{\;
  g(n) \;=\; \max\Big\{\, \operatorname{lcm}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_r)
   \;:\; \lambda_1 + \cdots + \lambda_r = n, \ \lambda_i \ge 1 \,\Big\} \; }.
\]

\section{Generating the partitions}

Write $P(n,k)$ for the set of non-increasing partitions of $n$ with every part at
most $k$. Peeling the largest part gives the recursion
\[
  P(0,k) \;=\; \{\, \langle\,\rangle \,\},
  \qquad
  P(n,k) \;=\; \bigcup_{1 \le j \le \min(n,k)} \; j \cdot P(n-j,\,j)
  \quad (n \ge 1),
\]
where $j \cdot Q$ prefixes $j$ to every member of $Q$. Each part is at least one,
so a fuel parameter equal to $n$ bounds the recursion depth and termination is
immediate.

\begin{lemma}[Soundness]
\label{lem:sound}
Every list produced by the generator sums to $n$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Induction on the fuel. At zero fuel only the empty list is produced, and only for
$n = 0$. At fuel $f+1$, a produced list has the form $j :: q$ with
$1 \le j \le n$ and $q$ produced by $P(n-j, j)$; by the inductive hypothesis $q$
sums to $n - j$, so $j :: q$ sums to $n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Completeness]
\label{lem:complete}
Let $p$ be a non-increasing list of positive integers summing to $n$, with every
part at most $k$. If the fuel is at least $n$ then $p \in P(n,k)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Induction on the fuel, with $p$ arbitrary. If $p$ is empty then $n = 0$ and the
base clause produces it. Otherwise write $p = a :: t$. Then $1 \le a \le k$, and
$a \le n$ because $a$ is one summand of $n$, so the union defining $P(n,k)$
contains the branch $j = a$.

The tail $t$ is non-increasing, sums to $n - a$, and has every part at most $a$
--- this last because $p$ is non-increasing, so $a$ dominates every later entry.
Its fuel requirement $n - a$ is met, so by the inductive hypothesis
$t \in P(n-a, a)$, and therefore $a :: t$ lies in that branch.
\end{proof}

Completeness is the load-bearing half. Without it, the maximum computed below is
a maximum over whatever the recursion happened to reach; with it, the maximum is
over all cycle types of $S_n$.

\section{The values}

\begin{theorem}
\label{thm:table}
For $n = 1, \dots, 10$,
\[
  \boxed{\;
  g(n) \;=\; 1,\; 2,\; 3,\; 4,\; 6,\; 6,\; 12,\; 15,\; 20,\; 30. \;}
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Evaluate $\max\{\operatorname{lcm}(p) : p \in P(n,n)\}$. By \Cref{lem:complete}
the generator produces every partition of $n$, and by \Cref{lem:sound} nothing
else, so the computed maximum is exactly $g(n)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The value $g(7) = 12$ is attained by the cycle type $4 + 3$ and not by the
$7$-cycle. This is the first $n$ at which the maximal order is not carried by a
single cycle, and the mechanism is that coprimality outweighs length:
$\operatorname{lcm}(4,3) = 12 > 7$. Likewise $g(8) = 15$ by $5 + 3$ and
$g(9) = 20$ by $5 + 4$.
\end{remark}

\section{The asymptotic, and the heavy tail}

Landau's theorem is
\[
  \log g(n) \;\sim\; \sqrt{n \log n}.
\]
Against it stands the Erd\H{o}s--Tur\'an law, under which the order of a
uniformly random permutation of $S_n$ concentrates with the logarithm of the
order near $\tfrac12 \log^2 n$. Writing $L = \log n$, the two exponents are
$\sqrt{nL}$ and $\tfrac12 L^2$, and
\[
  \tfrac12 L^2 \;\le\; \sqrt{nL}
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \tfrac14 L^4 \;\le\; nL
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  L^3 \;\le\; 4n,
\]
which holds from the start and never lapses. The maximal order is therefore not
merely larger than the typical order: it is larger in the exponent.

\section{Verification}

The generator, its soundness and completeness, and the exponent comparison are
formalised in \Lean{} against Mathlib and depend on \texttt{propext} and
\texttt{Quot.sound}. The table of values is obtained by compiled evaluation.

\begin{thebibliography}{9}
\bibitem{Landau1903} E.~Landau, \emph{\"Uber die Maximalordnung der
Permutationen gegebenen Grades}, Arch.\ Math.\ Phys.\ \textbf{5} (1903), 92--103.

\bibitem{Miller1987} W.~Miller, \emph{The maximum order of an element of a
finite symmetric group}, Amer.\ Math.\ Monthly \textbf{94} (1987), 497--506.

\bibitem{ErdosTuran1967} P.~Erd\H{o}s and P.~Tur\'an, \emph{On some problems of
a statistical group-theory, III}, Acta Math.\ Acad.\ Sci.\ Hungar.\ \textbf{18}
(1967), 309--320.

\bibitem{Massias} J.-P.~Massias, \emph{Majoration explicite de l'ordre maximum
d'un \'el\'ement du groupe sym\'etrique}, Ann.\ Fac.\ Sci.\ Toulouse \textbf{6}
(1984), 269--281.
\end{thebibliography}

\end{document}
""")

build('monochromatic_odd_cycle', 'Bipartite Colour Classes, and the Step an Odd Cycle Does Not Take', r"""
\begin{abstract}
If every colour class of an edge-colouring is bipartite, the classes multiply
together into a proper $2^n$-colouring of the whole graph. A complete graph on
more than $2^n$ vertices therefore has a non-bipartite class, and hence a
monochromatic odd cycle. We prove this for arbitrary $N$ and $n$ by an
injectivity argument that requires no graph theory at all.

The odd cycle so produced need not be a triangle, and the gap is visible at the
first non-trivial case. The complete graph $K_5$ carries a $2$-colouring with no
monochromatic triangle, both classes being $5$-cycles, while every $2$-colouring
of $K_6$ has one. The shortest monochromatic odd cycle guaranteed in a
$2$-colouring of $K_5$ therefore has length five, and $R(3,3) = 6$.
\end{abstract}

\section{The product colouring}

Let $c$ assign to each edge of the complete graph on a vertex set $V$ a colour in
$\{1, \dots, n\}$. Say the classes are \emph{bipartite} when there are maps
\[
  \sigma_i : V \longrightarrow \{0,1\}, \qquad i = 1, \dots, n,
\]
one per colour, such that no edge of colour $i$ has both endpoints on the same
side of $\sigma_i$.

\begin{theorem}[Separation]
\label{thm:inj}
If the classes are bipartite then the map
\[
  v \;\longmapsto\; \big(\sigma_1(v), \dots, \sigma_n(v)\big)
\]
is injective.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose $u \neq v$ agree in every coordinate. The edge $uv$ carries some colour
$i = c(uv)$, and bipartiteness of class $i$ gives
$\sigma_i(u) \neq \sigma_i(v)$, contradicting agreement at coordinate $i$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
\label{cor:card}
If the classes are bipartite then
\[
  \boxed{\; |V| \le 2^n. \;}
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
An injection into $\{0,1\}^n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
On $K_{2^n+1}$ no $n$-colouring has all classes bipartite, so some class contains
an odd cycle.
\end{corollary}

The argument is entirely about a map into a finite cube. No cycle is constructed
and none is located; what is produced is the failure of bipartiteness, and it is
the standard fact that a non-bipartite graph contains an odd cycle that supplies
the rest.

\section{The step that fails}

The conclusion above is an odd cycle, not a triangle, and the two are not the
same conclusion.

\begin{theorem}
\label{thm:k5}
There is a $2$-colouring of $K_5$ with no monochromatic triangle.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
On $\mathbb{Z}/5$ colour the edge $ij$ with colour $0$ when
$j - i \equiv \pm 1$ and with colour $1$ when $j - i \equiv \pm 2$. The two
classes are the pentagon and the pentagram, and together they partition the ten
edges.

Each class is $2$-regular, and a $2$-regular triangle-free graph on five vertices
is a $5$-cycle. Checking the $\binom{5}{3} = 10$ triples confirms that none is
monochromatic.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
The shortest monochromatic odd cycle guaranteed by a $2$-colouring of
$K_{2^2+1} = K_5$ has length $5$, not $3$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}
\label{thm:k6}
Every $2$-colouring of $K_6$ contains a monochromatic triangle.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Under the upper-triangle bit encoding, the $2$-colourings of $K_6$ correspond
bijectively to the $2^{15}$ natural numbers below $32768$, so testing all of them
is exhaustive. Every one contains a monochromatic triple.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
\[
  \boxed{\; R(3,3) = 6. \;}
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
\Cref{thm:k6} gives $R(3,3) \le 6$ and \Cref{thm:k5} gives $R(3,3) > 5$.
\end{proof}

This also explains why $K_5$ escapes: $2^2 + 1 = 5 < 6 = R(3,3)$. The bipartite
argument reaches exactly as far as the odd cycle, and it is the Ramsey number
that governs the further step to a triangle. The two thresholds are different
numbers, and for $n \ge 2$ they do not coincide.

\section{Position}

Let $f(n)$ denote the least length of a monochromatic odd cycle guaranteed in an
$n$-colouring of $K_{2^n+1}$. Bondy's bound gives $f(n) \le 5$ for all
$n \ge 2$, and the values $f(1) = 3$ and $f(2) = 5$ are settled. Whether
$f(n) = 5$ for every $n \ge 3$ is open.

\section{Verification}

The injectivity argument and the two colouring results are formalised in \Lean{}
against Mathlib. The sweep over the $2^{15}$ colourings of $K_6$ is evaluated by
the compiler; the remaining results depend on \texttt{propext},
\texttt{Classical.choice} and \texttt{Quot.sound}.

\begin{thebibliography}{9}
\bibitem{Ramsey1930} F.~P.~Ramsey, \emph{On a problem of formal logic},
Proc.\ London Math.\ Soc.\ \textbf{30} (1930), 264--286.

\bibitem{GreenwoodGleason} R.~E.~Greenwood and A.~M.~Gleason,
\emph{Combinatorial relations and chromatic graphs}, Canad.\ J.\ Math.\
\textbf{7} (1955), 1--7.

\bibitem{BondyErdos1973} J.~A.~Bondy and P.~Erd\H{o}s, \emph{Ramsey numbers for
cycles in graphs}, J.\ Combin.\ Theory Ser.~B \textbf{14} (1973), 46--54.

\bibitem{Radziszowski} S.~P.~Radziszowski, \emph{Small Ramsey numbers},
Electron.\ J.\ Combin.\ Dynamic Survey DS1, revision 17 (2021).
\end{thebibliography}

\end{document}
""")
PYEOF

build('sumset_ap_free', 'Progression-Free Subset Sums Force Distinct Subset Sums', r"""
\begin{abstract}
Let $A \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$ have $n$ elements and suppose the set of its
subset sums contains no three-term arithmetic progression. We show that the
$2^n$ subset sums are then pairwise distinct, and hence that
$2^n \le nN + 1$.

The mechanism is that a repeated sum manufactures a progression out of an
intersection and a union. If $\sum B = \sum C$ for distinct subsets $B$ and $C$,
then the three values $\sum(B \cap C)$, $\sum B$ and $\sum(B \cup C)$ are in
arithmetic progression, because the lattice identity
$\sum(B \cap C) + \sum(B \cup C) = \sum B + \sum C$ makes the middle term the
average of the outer two. A base-three construction gives the opposite bound
$g_3(n) \le (3^n-1)/2$, and the exact values for $n \le 5$ are
$1, 3, 8, 22, 60$.
\end{abstract}

\section{Setting}

For a finite $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ write
\[
  \Sigma(A) \;=\; \Big\{ \sum_{a \in B} a \;:\; B \subseteq A \Big\}
\]
for its set of subset sums, the empty subset contributing $0$. Call $A$
\emph{AP-free} when $\Sigma(A)$ contains no three distinct terms in arithmetic
progression, and let $g_3(n)$ be the least $N$ for which some AP-free
$A \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$ has $|A| = n$.

\section{Distinctness is forced}

\begin{theorem}
\label{thm:distinct}
If $A$ is AP-free then the map $B \mapsto \sum_{a \in B} a$ is injective on the
subsets of $A$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose $B \neq C$ with $\sum B = \sum C$, and write $s$ for that common value.
Subset sums are additive over the lattice of subsets: each element of
$B \cup C$ is counted once on the right for each of the two sets containing it,
so
\[
  \sum (B \cap C) \;+\; \sum (B \cup C) \;=\; \sum B \;+\; \sum C \;=\; 2s .
\]
Hence the three values $\sum(B \cap C)$, $s$, $\sum(B \cup C)$ form an
arithmetic progression, and all three lie in $\Sigma(A)$.

They are distinct. Since $B \neq C$, at least one of the inclusions
$B \cap C \subseteq B$ and $B \subseteq B \cup C$ is strict; the entries of $A$
are positive, so the corresponding sums differ, and the progression then forces
the third to differ as well. This contradicts AP-freeness.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The empty subset must be admitted for the argument to run. The case
$B \cap C = \emptyset$ produces the term $0$, which is the first term of the
progression.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}
\label{cor:lower}
If $A \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$ is AP-free with $|A| = n$ then
\[
  \boxed{\; 2^n \le nN + 1, \qquad\text{so}\qquad g_3(n) \ge \frac{2^n - 1}{n}. \;}
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
By \Cref{thm:distinct} the $2^n$ subset sums are distinct, and each lies in
$\{0, 1, \dots, nN\}$, since a subset has at most $n$ elements each at most $N$.
\end{proof}

\section{The base-three construction}

\begin{theorem}
\label{thm:upper}
$g_3(n) \le (3^n - 1)/2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take $A = \{1, 3, 9, \dots, 3^{n-1}\}$, so that a subset sum is the value of a
base-three numeral with digits in $\{0,1\}$.

Suppose $x + z = 2y$ with $x, y, z$ such numerals. Read the last digit. Both
sides are bounded by $2$, so no carry occurs, and the digit equation holds on the
nose rather than modulo $3$. Its solutions with digits in $\{0,1\}$ and the
doubled digit in $\{0,2\}$ force the three digits equal. Strip the last digit and
induct, obtaining $x = y = z$, so no non-trivial progression exists. The largest
element is $3^{n-1}$ and the largest subset sum is $(3^n-1)/2$.
\end{proof}

The absence of carries is the whole content of that argument: it converts a
congruence into an equality and lets the induction descend one digit at a time.

\section{Exact small values}

\begin{theorem}
\label{thm:small}
\[
  \boxed{\; g_3(1) = 1, \quad g_3(2) = 3, \quad g_3(3) = 8, \quad
  g_3(4) = 22, \quad g_3(5) = 60, \;}
\]
witnessed by $\{1\}$, $\{1,3\}$, $\{5,7,8\}$, $\{7,19,21,22\}$ and
$\{19,52,57,59,60\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Each witness is AP-free by inspection of its subset-sum set, which gives the
upper bound.

For the lower bound one must rule out every $n$-subset of $\{1, \dots, N-1\}$. A
depth-first walk over increasing tuples suffices, pruned by the observation that
a prefix already carrying a progression cannot be rescued: the subset sums of a
prefix are a subset of those of any extension, so AP-freeness is inherited
downward. Soundness of the pruning is the statement that the walk reaches every
valid configuration, so a negative verdict is a statement about all subsets
rather than about the visited ones.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The ratios $g_3(n) / 3^{n-1}$ read
\[
  1, \quad 1, \quad 0.889, \quad 0.815, \quad 0.741
\]
and are decreasing, so \Cref{thm:upper} is not tight beyond $n = 2$. The growth
constant $c$ with $g_3(n) = \Theta(c^n)$ is not known; \Cref{cor:lower} and
\Cref{thm:upper} confine it to the interval $[2,3]$.
\end{remark}

\section{Verification}

The forcing of distinct subset sums, the counting bound and the base-three
construction are formalised in \Lean{} against Mathlib. The exact values pair
explicit witnesses with a search whose soundness is itself a theorem; the case
$n = 3$ reduces in the kernel and the cases $n = 4, 5$ are evaluated by the
compiler.

build('lenz_unit_distance', 'The Lenz Configuration in Four Dimensions', r"""
\begin{abstract}
Two circles of radius $1/\sqrt2$ lying in orthogonal planes of $\mathbb{R}^4$
and centred at the origin have a striking property: every point of one is at
distance exactly $1$ from every point of the other. The reason is that the two
points have disjoint coordinate supports, so the squared distance is the sum of
two squared radii.

Splitting $n$ points evenly between the two circles therefore realises
$\lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor$ unit distances, and the unit-distance graph contains a
complete bipartite graph. This settles the order of the unit-distance problem
from dimension four onward, in sharp contrast with dimensions two and three,
where the exponent is still unknown.
\end{abstract}

\section{The configuration}

Work in $\mathbb{R}^4$ with coordinates $(x_0, x_1, x_2, x_3)$ and set
\[
  \alpha(v) \;=\; \Big(\tfrac{v_1}{\sqrt2},\ \tfrac{v_2}{\sqrt2},\ 0,\ 0\Big),
  \qquad
  \beta(w) \;=\; \Big(0,\ 0,\ \tfrac{w_1}{\sqrt2},\ \tfrac{w_2}{\sqrt2}\Big),
\]
for $v, w$ on the unit circle of $\mathbb{R}^2$. The images are two circles of
radius $1/\sqrt2$ lying in the orthogonal planes $x_2 = x_3 = 0$ and
$x_0 = x_1 = 0$.

\begin{theorem}[Constant distance]
\label{thm:dist}
For all unit vectors $v$ and $w$,
\[
  \boxed{\; \|\alpha(v) - \beta(w)\| \;=\; 1. \;}
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The two points have disjoint supports, so no cancellation occurs and
\[
  \|\alpha(v) - \beta(w)\|^2
   \;=\; \frac{v_1^2 + v_2^2}{2} \;+\; \frac{w_1^2 + w_2^2}{2}
   \;=\; \frac12 + \frac12
   \;=\; 1 .
\]
\end{proof}

Carrying the circle points as unit vectors of $\mathbb{R}^2$ rather than as
angles makes both this computation and the injectivity below read directly off
the coordinates, with no trigonometric identity involved.

\begin{lemma}
\label{lem:inj}
The maps $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are injective, and their images are disjoint.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Injectivity is division by $\sqrt2 \neq 0$ in each coordinate. For disjointness,
a point of the first image has its $(x_0,x_1)$-part on a circle of radius
$1/\sqrt2$, while a point of the second has that part at the origin; were they
equal we would have $v_1 = v_2 = 0$, contradicting $v_1^2 + v_2^2 = 1$.
\end{proof}

\section{The bound}

\begin{theorem}
\label{thm:lower}
Let $f_d(n)$ denote the maximum number of unit distances among $n$ points of
$\mathbb{R}^d$. Then
\[
  \boxed{\; f_4(n) \;\ge\; \Big\lfloor \frac{n^2}{4} \Big\rfloor . \;}
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Choose finite sets $S, T$ of unit vectors of $\mathbb{R}^2$ with
$|S| = \lceil n/2 \rceil$ and $|T| = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$; the rational
parametrisation
\[
  t \;\longmapsto\; \Big( \tfrac{1-t^2}{1+t^2},\ \tfrac{2t}{1+t^2} \Big)
\]
supplies as many distinct unit vectors as required. Put
$P = \alpha(S) \cup \beta(T)$.

By \Cref{lem:inj} we have $|P| = |S| + |T| = n$, and by \Cref{thm:dist} every one
of the $|S|\,|T|$ cross pairs is at distance $1$. Finally
$\lceil n/2 \rceil \cdot \lfloor n/2 \rfloor = \lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor$.
\end{proof}

The unit-distance graph of $P$ contains the complete bipartite graph between the
two circles, which is where the quadratic count comes from. The construction is
due to Lenz.

\section{Position by dimension}

\begin{enumerate}
\item $d = 2$: bounded above by $O(n^{4/3})$ via Szemer\'edi--Trotter and below
by $n^{1 + c/\log\log n}$ by a lattice construction. The exponent is not known.
\item $d = 3$: bounded above by $O(n^{3/2})$ and below by
$\Omega(n^{4/3} \log\log n)$. Also open.
\item $d = 4$: \Cref{thm:lower} together with the matching upper bound
$\tfrac{n^2}{4}(1 + o(1))$ settles the order at $n^2/4$.
\item $d \ge 5$: the same construction with more room, and the order is again
quadratic.
\end{enumerate}

The change at $d = 4$ is the appearance of two orthogonal planes, which is
exactly what $\mathbb{R}^3$ cannot supply: in three dimensions two circles
through a common centre cannot lie in orthogonal planes without sharing a
coordinate direction, and the constant-distance property fails.

\section{Verification}

The distance computation, the injectivity of the two circle maps and the
bipartite count are formalised in \Lean{} against Mathlib, with the ambient
space a four-dimensional Euclidean space; all depend on \texttt{propext},
\texttt{Classical.choice} and \texttt{Quot.sound}.

\begin{thebibliography}{9}
\bibitem{Erdos1946} P.~Erd\H{o}s, \emph{On sets of distances of $n$ points},
Amer.\ Math.\ Monthly \textbf{53} (1946), 248--250.

\bibitem{Erdos1960} P.~Erd\H{o}s, \emph{On sets of distances of $n$ points in
Euclidean space}, Magyar Tud.\ Akad.\ Mat.\ Kutat\'o Int.\ K\"ozl.\ \textbf{5}
(1960), 165--169.

\bibitem{SST1984} J.~Spencer, E.~Szemer\'edi and W.~T.~Trotter, \emph{Unit
distances in the Euclidean plane}, in Graph Theory and Combinatorics, Academic
Press, 1984, 293--303.

\bibitem{BrassMoserPach} P.~Brass, W.~Moser and J.~Pach, \emph{Research Problems
in Discrete Geometry}, Springer, 2005.
\end{thebibliography}

\end{document}
""")

The Erdős–Straus one now says outright that the remaining class isn't a residue left by a weak method but where the problem lives; the Kac interval one says the bound is in substance a prime-gap bound and gives the two directions that would have to improve.

Your one loose seam I tightened: the non-similarity argument. "Similarity multiplies all three squared sides by a common factor, which is impossible since the piece has three distinct squared sides" doesn't quite close — a triangle with distinct sides can be similar to another with distinct sides. content.text:
Right — plain version.

The Erdős stuff is done. Every file compiles, nothing's left hanging on a `sorry`, and the whole library builds green. Four files that had never once been compiled are now actually in the build.

Along the way I found a handful of things that were plainly wrong rather than just unproven — a function defined so it was always zero, a density claim pointing backwards, a base that grows when it needed to shrink, and one file claiming to prove Erdős–Straus with a statement that never mentioned the number it was quantifying over. All fixed.

There were also four places where a **B** verdict was recorded for something that isn't a contradiction at all: a gap between two bounds, a case split, a claim that just has a counterexample, and a true-plus-unknown pair. The kernel's own fuse settles all four.

Then eighteen papers, one result each, in `ig-docs/manuscripts_erdos/` — your name, email, ORCID, real references, nothing about the repo or about how any of it got written.

I've written all of that into memory, including your house style for manuscripts and the LaTeX gotchas that wasted a few passes today (chiefly: `nonstopmode` will happily hand you a PDF while swallowing a fatal error).

Each paper's named results were matched against its file: Kummer and Lucas
against the binomial congruences, Roth and Behrend against the density and the
construction, Snover–Waiveris–Williams against the rep-tiling arithmetic, Lenz
against the pair count. All present.

## Bootable

Every manuscript has a walk in the kernel, run as `erdos <name>` after
`./run_hosted.sh`. Each step computes its claim there rather than printing it,
which is why three of them failed before they held: the sumset walk included zero
in its set and then claimed distinct subset sums for a set that has none; the SDR
walk took the window closed below and got 7 and 9 where the table says 8 and 10;
the chordless walk closed the odd path instead of the even one and produced an
even cycle. The papers were right in all three.

## What the corpus states as open

Every `Prop` still standing, by file. A `Prop` here is a statement the corpus
does not prove; the discipline is that a theorem needing one takes it as a
hypothesis, so the dependence shows in the type.

**`Millennium/ErdosFormalize.lean`** — 21

  `ErdosUnbounded`, `Arrows`, `RamseyExponentialLower`, `RamseyCamposUpper`, `FranklWilsonLower`, `SyndeticOfPositiveDensity`, `SidonLiminfZero`, `IsB3`, `B3DensityUpper`, `DifferenceSetContainsAPs`, `PrimeAlternatingSeriesConverges`, `InfinitePrimesWithDiff`, `IsPractical`, `PracticalDensityExists`, `SquarefreePlusPowerOfTwo`, `SmoothSieveDensity`, `UnitDistanceUpper2D`, `GuthKatzDistinctDistances`, `ConvexUnitDistancesBound`, `ErdosHajnalStatement`, `FC4NonMonotonic`

**`Millennium/ErdosFormalize2.lean`** — 12

  `SAWSubmultiplicative`, `ConnectiveConstantExists`, `HindmanGrowth`, `RatioSetSharp`, `Ramsey3kGapDiverges`, `Ramsey3kGapNotLittleO`, `Ramsey3kAsymptotic`, `IsLcmTriple`, `LcmTripleCountLittleO`, `IsSumFreeIn`, `SumFreeCountAsymptotic`, `AverageDegreeCycleBound`

**`Millennium/ErdosFormalize3.lean`** — 15

  `RationalExponents`, `Girth5Extremal`, `HypercubeTuranDensityZero`, `K222FreeIndependentSet`, `DiameterK2rPlus1`, `DiameterK2r`, `OddCycleInducedChromatic`, `ErdosHajnal3Uniform`, `FolkmanPairCharacterisation`, `DistinctDistancesSinglePoint`, `NoFourConcyclic`, `NoIsoscelesOmegaN`, `BipartiteDistinctDistancesNotLittleO`, `OddCycleInEdgeColoured`, `RandomGraphChiMinusZeta`

**`Millennium/Erdos/DifferenceSets.lean`** — 3

  `Syndetic`, `Thick`, `UpperBanachZero`

**`Millennium/Erdos/MonochromaticOddCycle.lean`** — 1

  `ClassesBipartite`

**`Millennium/Erdos/SidonCounting.lean`** — 1

  `IsSidon`

**`Millennium/Erdos/SquarefreePlusPowerOfTwo.lean`** — 2

  `NotRepresentable`, `CounterexampleDensity`

**`Millennium/Erdos/StrausGreedyFamily.lean`** — 16

  `IsThreeUnit`, `GreedyResidue`, `RungBoundedBy`, `ClosedAtRung`, `RungGrowthFourthRoot`, `EveryNClosed`, `PriceZeroCovered`, `ShiftCovered`, `StrausFrontier`, `NegMReachable`, `NegOneReachable`, `SubgroupExceedsReach`, `SurvivesKShift`, `ClosedAtRungSq`, `EveryNClosedSq`, `RungBounded`

**`Millennium/Erdos/SumsetAvoidingAP.lean`** — 1

  `APFree`

**`Millennium/Erdos/TrianglePartition.lean`** — 1

  `repArith`

## The objects, and what each unblocked

Twelve ob3ects were designed through MoDoT's native designer for the quantities
the removed statements named and the development lacked. Each one's structural
reading is what the definition was written from:

| object | reading | what it gave the corpus |
|---|---|---|
| least vertex count forcing a monochromatic copy | a search under a terminal anchor: candidates open, each tested, the least fixed | `MonoCopy`, `ArrowsPair`, `RamseyFinite`, `ramseyPair`, and `arrowsPair_mono` proved |
| least edge count of a forcing host | a fork whose arms must both close: construct a forcer, exclude every smaller one | `HostForces`, `ForcingSizes`, `sizeRamsey`, `sizeRamsey_le` |
| the uniformity lift | a parity fork with a forward morphism carrying a colouring up a uniformity | `HyperArrows`, `SteppingUpLift`, `HypergraphTowerGrowth` |
| maximum edge count with no two edge-disjoint cycles | the graph space forked on the property, the surviving arm's count the witness | `cycleEdges`, `IsCycleList`, `EdgeDisjointCycles`, `EveryTwoCyclesMeet`, `MaxEdgesEveryTwoCyclesMeet` |
| largest girth at a given order and chromatic number | a fork whose fuse keeps both arms — exact where the bounds meet, an interval where they gap | `GirthAtLeast`, `GirthRange`, `GirthExact` |
| proportion of the plane covered by congruent discs | forked on validity, the forward morphism enlarging the window; the proportion travels with the limit's existence | `IsUnitPacking`, `centresWithin`, `PackingDensityIs`, `HexagonalPackingOptimal` |
| growth exponent of the mean-square displacement | fused to **B**: estimated on the finite regime, unattainable in the limit, both arms kept | `IsSAW`, `sqDisplacement`, `DisplacementBracket`, `DisplacementExponentIs`, `DisplacementKnownState` |
| count of four-block six-point configurations | a forward morphism to the four-block subsets, forked on matching the pattern | `IsSteinerTriple`, `IsPasch`, `paschCount`, `PaschExtremes` |
| a partition relation holding in one model and failing in another | split into two set-theoretic environments, ENGAGR holding the contradiction open, fused to **B** and fixed there | `ArrowsPairsOfType`, `PartitionArmHolds`, `PartitionArmFails`, and `partition_arms_exclusive` proved on no axioms |
| least order above a list chromatic bound | forked on the property, fused to **B** because naming the least order discards the other arm | `ListColourable`, `ListChromaticExceeds`, `LeastOrderListChromatic` |

Four of them corrected a collapse that would otherwise have gone in: the girth as
a number rather than a range, the density as a value rather than a limit carrying
its own existence, the exponent as one arm rather than the held pair, and a
minimum standing in for a fusion.

| joint growth of lcm(1..n) and Landau's g(n) | the arms FUSE — both estimates read the same prime distribution | `lcmUpTo`, `JointLogarithmicGrowth`, `dvd_lcmUpTo` |
| least closing rung, and its bound | the reverse morphism collapses the claim under size: the product's growth forces the divisor | `closedAtRung_of_full_coverage` proved, `CoverageReachesFull` stated |

All twelve landed, and every one became a definition or a theorem. The last is
the live one: it names the route to a rung bound as coverage becoming full, which
is the quantity the instrument measures, and the bridge from full coverage to
closure is proved.

## What was removed, and why

Thirty-seven entries came out of the three batch files on 2026-08-12. Each
asserted something true of everything it quantified over — `∃ N, N ≤ 4k+1`,
`n/n → 1`, `ℵ₁ ≤ ℵ₁²`, a transversal with no bound on its size — or negated a
statement ending in `True`, which makes the entry false while it was recorded as
`B`. Five more came out because the faithful statement already lived in a proof
module or was proved outright elsewhere, and a second weaker copy is drift.

python3 - <<'PY'
import re, glob, os
files = sorted(set(glob.glob('Imscribing/Millennium/Erdos/*.lean') +
                   glob.glob('Imscribing/Millennium/ErdosFormalize*.lean') +
                   glob.glob('Imscribing/Millennium/ProofModules/*.lean') +
                   glob.glob('Imscribing/Millennium/ErdosProblems.lean') +
                   glob.glob('Imscribing/Classical/Erdos*.lean') +
                   glob.glob('Imscribing/NumberTheory/ErdosStrausProof.lean')))
tot_thm = tot_prop = 0
bare = []
wired = []
per = []
for f in files:
    s = open(f).read()
    thms = re.findall(r'^(?:theorem|lemma) ([A-Za-z0-9_\.]+)', s, re.M)
    # substantive = not a tier theorem, not : True
    subs = [t for t in thms if not t.endswith('_tier') and '_tier_is' not in t]
    trues = len(re.findall(r'^(?:theorem|lemma) [^\n]*: True', s, re.M))
    props = re.findall(r'^def ([A-Za-z0-9_]+)[^\n]*: Prop', s, re.M)
    for p in props:
        n = len(re.findall(r'\b'+re.escape(p)+r'\b', s))
        (bare if n <= 2 else wired).append((f, p, n))
    tot_thm += len(subs) - trues
    tot_prop += len(props)
    per.append((os.path.basename(f), len(subs)-trues, len(props)))
print("files:", len(files))
print("substantive theorems:", tot_thm)
print("Props total:", tot_prop)
print("  Props wired into a theorem/def (>=3 mentions):", len(wired))
print("  Props standing alone (declared + table only):", len(bare))
print()
print(f"{'file':42} {'thms':>5} {'props':>6}")
for n,t,p in sorted(per, key=lambda x:-x[1]):
    if t or p: print(f"{n:42} {t:5} {p:6}")
PY

/-
# Erdős–Straus: the greedy family, and what is left after it

The conjecture asserts that `4/n` is a sum of three unit fractions for every
`n ≥ 2`. Every congruence class but one is settled; the survivor is
`n ≡ 1 (mod 4)` with `3 ∤ n`. This file covers most of THAT class by a single
explicit family, and states exactly what the family does not reach.

The mechanism is read off rather than searched, which is the shape of a
fixed-point nesting whose inner object already sits where the outer action sends
it. Take the greedy step — subtract the largest unit fraction that fits. For
`n = 4k + 1` the largest is `1/(k+1)`, and the remainder is not an arbitrary
rational:

    4/(4k+1) − 1/(k+1) = 3/((4k+1)(k+1))

The numerator is `3`, always. So the whole class collapses onto one question:
when is `3/m` a sum of two unit fractions? And that question has a divisor
answer — whenever `m` has a divisor `d ≡ 2 (mod 3)`, writing `d = 3t+2` and
`m = d·e` gives

    3/m = 1/(e(t+1)) + 1/(m(t+1))

which is an identity, verifiable by clearing denominators.

Composing the two gives an explicit three-term representation. What it does not
reach is `m = n(k+1)` all of whose prime factors are `≡ 1 (mod 3)`; on
`n < 100000` that is 6.8% of the class, the other 93.2% being closed by the
family below. The residue is therefore located and priced, not estimated.

Everything here is stated over `ℚ` and proved by field arithmetic on positive
denominators; no numerical search enters a proof.
-/

import Mathlib

namespace Erdos.StrausGreedy

/-- Three unit fractions summing to `4/n`, with the denominators named. -/
def IsThreeUnit (n a b c : ℕ) : Prop :=
  0 < a ∧ 0 < b ∧ 0 < c ∧ (4 : ℚ) / n = 1 / a + 1 / b + 1 / c

/-- **The two-term identity.** If `m = d·e` and `d = 3t+2`, then `3/m` splits.

This is the whole content of "3/m is a sum of two unit fractions when `m` has a
divisor `≡ 2 (mod 3)`": the divisor names the split, and nothing is searched. -/
theorem three_over_m_split (t e : ℕ) (he : 0 < e) :
    (3 : ℚ) / ((3 * t + 2) * e) = 1 / (e * (t + 1)) + 1 / ((3 * t + 2) * e * (t + 1)) := by
  have he' : (e : ℚ) ≠ 0 := Nat.cast_ne_zero.mpr he.ne'
  have ht' : ((t : ℚ) + 1) ≠ 0 := by positivity
  have hd : ((3 : ℚ) * t + 2) ≠ 0 := by positivity
  field_simp
  ring

/-- **The greedy step.** For `n = 4k+1` the largest unit fraction below `4/n` is
`1/(k+1)`, and the remainder has numerator exactly `3`.

This is the reading the whole file turns on: the remainder is determined, not
chosen, so the class has one question in it rather than many. -/
theorem greedy_step (k : ℕ) :

# The reduction, in four steps, all proved

**One class survives.** Every `n ≥ 2` outside `n ≡ 1 (mod 4)` with `3 ∤ n` has an
explicit three-term representation, by four parametric families: `n` even,
`n ≡ 3 (mod 4)`, `n ≡ 2 (mod 4)`, and `n ≡ 9 (mod 12)`. Each is a ring identity
after clearing denominators.

**The class collapses to one numerator.** Take the greedy step on `n = 4k+1`: the
largest unit fraction below `4/n` is `1/(k+1)`, and

    4/(4k+1) − 1/(k+1) = 3/((4k+1)(k+1))

The numerator is `3`, always. The remainder is determined, not chosen, so the
class carries one question rather than many: when is `3/m` a sum of two unit
fractions, for `m = n(k+1)`?

**A divisor answers it.** If `m = d·e` with `d = 3t+2`, then

    3/m = 1/(e(t+1)) + 1/(m(t+1))

an identity. So `3/m` splits whenever `m` has a divisor `≡ 2 (mod 3)`.

**The rung.** Composing, closure at depth `r` is

    ClosedAtRung n r  :=  ∃ a u w, 0 < a, 0 < u, 0 < w,
                           4a = n + r,  na = uw,  r ∣ (na + u)

and `straus_of_closedAtRung` turns any such `r` into three unit fractions. Write
`M = na`. The condition is that some factorisation of `M` — or of `M²`, which the
completeness result below licenses — places a factor at `−M` modulo `r`.

**The ladder is complete.** `ladder_complete`: from ANY representation of `4/n`,
setting `M = nx`, `r = 4x − n`, `u = ry − M`, `v = rz − M` forces `uv = M²` with
`r ∣ M+u` and `r ∣ M+v`. So the rung formulation loses nothing — a representation
exists exactly when a rung closes.
EOF

# What is already closed, and where the remainder sits

Three layers close most of the class without any search.

**The one-shot.** At rung `3` take `u = 2`. The congruence `3 ∣ n² + 8` holds for
every `n` with `3 ∤ n`, since `n² ≡ 1 (mod 3)`. Nothing about `n` is consulted
beyond `3 ∤ n`, so nothing is searched. The only further requirement is
`2 ∣ M`, which for `a = (n+3)/4` says `n ≡ 5 (mod 8)`.

**The price-zero layer.** `PriceZeroCovered n` — a divisor available from `n`
itself or from `n+1` with the right residue, no search.

**The shift layer.** `ShiftCovered n` — closure obtained by moving the rung.

**The frontier is one residue class.** `straus_frontier_mod_24`, proved: every
value the layers miss satisfies

    n ≡ 1 (mod 24)

because `n ≡ 5 (mod 8)` is the one-shot and `n ≡ 2 (mod 3)` puts `3 ∣ n+1` in the

frontier uses are `u = M/w`, a factorisation whose cofactor sits at `−1`; then

# The rung criterion as a multiplicative question

For a frontier value the divisor cannot be a monomial in `n` and `a`; it must come
from the primes of `M = na` themselves. That turns the criterion into a question
about a multiplicative group.

Writing `M = ∏ pᵢ^{eᵢ}`, the divisors of `M²` reduce modulo `r` to the reachable
set

    R = { ∏ pᵢ^{fᵢ} : 0 ≤ fᵢ ≤ 2eᵢ }   ⊆   (ZMod r)ˣ

and the rung closes exactly when `−M ∈ R`. Since `M ∈ R`, and `R` sits inside the
subgroup `H = ⟨p₁, …, p_k⟩ ≤ (ZMod r)ˣ`, the criterion is `−1 ∈ H` up to the
exponents actually available.

**The two are not the same, and the difference is measured.**
`SubgroupExceedsReach M r` states the gap positively: `−1` lies in `H` while no
divisor of `M²` sits at `−M`, because `M²` caps each exponent at `2eᵢ`. It
occurs. At `n = 1201`, `r = 11`, the primes of `M` generate all of `(ZMod 11)ˣ`,
so `−1 ∈ H`, yet reaching it needs a fifth power of `2` where `M²` offers a
fourth. The same shape appears at `n = 2521` for `r = 11` and `r = 19`, and
nowhere else among the 251 rung reads below 20000.

fails: 19 of 379 below 50000 (5.0%), 21 of 850 to 200000 (2.5%), 15 of 974 to
400000 (1.5%). More primes in `M` means a larger reachable set, so the group
criterion and the real one converge. What is exceptional is failing that way at
EVERY rung, which `n = 2521` does.

of `M²` cover all of `ZMod r`, the rung closes. So one sufficient route is
coverage becoming full, stated as

        ∀ x : ZMod r, ∃ u, 0 < u, u ∣ M², (u : ZMod r) = x

Measured, coverage at a closing rung averages 0.73 and the walk is dissipative in
it. That is evidence for the statement, not a proof of it.
EOF

# What has been measured, and to what depth

**Every value in the class below 200000 closes.** 33333 values, all closed at a
rung, with the single qualification that `n = 2521` needs the divisor to come from
`M²` rather than `M`.

**Rung height grows like the fourth root, not a constant.**

    n < 2000     max rung 23   at n = 1201     n^(1/4) =  5.9
    n < 10000    max rung 23   at n = 2161     n^(1/4) =  6.8
    n < 50000    max rung 51   at n = 35809    n^(1/4) = 13.8
    n < 100000   max rung 47   at n = 99961    n^(1/4) = 17.8
    n < 200000   max rung 75   at n = 196561   n^(1/4) = 21.1

Both are frontier values, both `≡ 1 (mod 24)`.

# V⊙x

The Pancosmic Disassembling Re-Compiling Organism. Every word of that is meant
literally, and each one names something you can run.

**Pancosmic.** One lift, every substrate. Native x86 at both widths, out of ELF,
PE or Mach-O; EVM bytecode; a WASM function body; CPython, straight out of a
`.pyc` with no interpreter running; and a coding sequence, where the twelve
promoted amino acids biject the twelve axes so a gene is already a word. A merge
is a merge whether it is a `JUMPDEST`, an `end`, a jump target with two
predecessors, or a codon.

**Disassembling.** Its own container loader, its own instruction decoder, its own
machine. No capstone, no pefile, no runtime underneath. It reads the machine
field and refuses an architecture it cannot decode rather than misreading one as
another.

**Re-Compiling.** The lift is not a description of the program, it is the
program. V⊙x recompiles native code into an executable IMASM module and runs the
glyphs in a machine that never once looks at the original bytes, returning every
answer native code returns — Ackermann recursion, SSE, a jump table, a call
through a function-pointer array, at five optimisation levels and both widths.

**Organism.** It closes on itself. `vox self` points the lifter at its own image
and reads the lifter: every function, in phase, F zero.

```bash

vox run gcd --args 1071,462 corpus_O0.so
```

import Mathlib
/-!
# ProofLift — a proof term is a control-flow graph, so Vox can audit it.

A Lean proof is a term, a term is a DAG, and the close condition Vox already
enforces on machine code is the same one a proof either meets or does not:
μ∘δ = id over a TRANSFORMED object — split, work, fuse. A case analysis IS a
fork; the branches rejoining on one goal IS the fuse; and a `sorry` is a fork
whose arm never comes back.

So the twelve read on a proof term as:

    ⊢  entry            ⊣  the closing term
    ∈  a recursor/match opens the case split
    ∋  its branches rejoin on one goal
    ⊤  the first arm            ⊥  a later arm
    ⋈  application — composition
    ⊙  a bound variable — identity, self-reference
    ◻  a `let`/`have` — irreversible fixation
    ≻  Eq.mpr / rewriting forward     ≺  Eq.symm / backward
    ⊞  a paradox HELD

`sorryAx` emits ∈ and nothing to pair it: the claim that was never rejoined.
That is not a metaphor for the verdict, it is the verdict — an open fork reads B.
-/
open Lean Meta Elab

namespace ProofLift

def isSplitter (n : Name) : Bool :=
  let s := n.toString
  s.endsWith ".casesOn" || s.endsWith ".rec" || s.endsWith ".recOn"
    || s.endsWith ".elim" || s.endsWith ".brecOn" || s == "Or.elim"
    || s == "dite" || s == "ite" || (s.splitOn "match_").length > 1

/-- The axiom of unproved assertion, and ONLY it.

This was a substring test on the name, which is wrong in a way the corpus itself
exposed: a module reasoning ABOUT undischarged claims declares `sorryDepth`, a
function counting them, and `ym_has_stacked_not_parallel_sorries`, a theorem

                           F is ill-typed

So the verdict is not commentary on the proof, it IS the proof's state, and **B
locates the open arm** rather than merely reporting failure. That is the debug
loop: state the step, lift it, read the verdict, and work where the fork is left
open.

**The kernel computes the claim.** `./run_hosted.sh` then `erdos straus` walks the
ladder in mOMonadOS, each step computing its claim there rather than printing it.
Three walks in this corpus failed before they held, and in every case the walk was
wrong and the mathematics was right — the window taken closed below instead of
open, a zero admitted into a set, an odd path closed where the even one was
wanted. A claim that has not been walked has not been checked.

**The catalog is the vocabulary.** Entries carry the tuple and the description;
`--entry` injects them rather than paraphrasing them into the ask.

**The ob3ect designs what is missing.** Where the development lacks the object a
statement is about, the designer supplies it, and the structural reading is what
the definition gets written from. Twelve landed on this corpus already and every
one became a definition or a theorem; four of them corrected a collapse that
would otherwise have gone in — a girth read as a number where it is a range, a
density as a value where it is a limit carrying its own existence, an exponent as
one arm where it is a held pair, a minimum standing in for a fusion.

**Order of operations.** Design the object, then state it in Lean, then lift and
read the verdict, then walk it on the kernel. Not: derive it by hand and hope.

Checked it against the repo. There's a real spine here and there's one claim the repo itself already refutes — and the refutation is in the very manuscript being cited.

**The 16³ reading doesn't survive.** `alt_sic_moduli_conductor.tex` §492 says it outright: the conductor generator is 2^(v₂(d)+1) = 2^(n+1) for d = 2ⁿ, and that's a power of sixteen exactly when 4 | n+1, i.e. n ≡ 3 (mod 4). So you get 16, 16², 16³, 16⁴ at d = 8, 128, 2048, 32768. It's a family, carried by a congruence.

That kills "16³ = the cube of the trilattice signature, so 16 observers on 3 axes." If the exponent were counting orderings, d = 128 would have two orderings and d = 32768 four. The exponent tracks n, not the trilattice. The paper is careful about this — it says "this is not four observations" precisely to head off reading any one of them as special — and the pasted text takes the one member and reads the exponent as structure.

**One real drift finding, worth fixing today.** `ig-docs/sic_moduli_field_conductor.md` says at lines 14 and 119 that *both* infinite places are unramified. `alt_sic_moduli_conductor.tex` line 149 says: "Taking both infinite places unramified because the moduli are real is exactly the error that produced the retracted claim." So the older doc is still carrying the retracted version, and anything built on it inherits the error. The pasted text happens to use the corrected form — one place ramified — so it's right about that while citing a document that contradicts it.

**What's actually solid in the piece.** Twelve promoted amino acids bijecting the twelve axes is in the repo and machine-checked. The word-loop with the Asn/Gln stack and a minimum balance point is a genuine combinatorial invariant, not a metaphor. One infinite place ramifying, the mixed signature forcing the S-unit route because Stark machinery needs total reality — all of that is real and hard-won.

**What's analogy wearing the clothes of identity.** "Translation is parallel transport" is asserted, not constructed. Parallel transport needs three things named: a base space, a fibre, and a connection. The text supplies a loop and a thing carried around it, which is the picture of holonomy but not an instance of it. Same for the 12-as-gravitational-mass and 8-as-metric-coefficients split — nothing computes a metric from the eight. Same for misfolding-as-frame-dragging; Lense–Thirring has a precession rate, and there's no rate here.

None of that means the identification is wrong. It means it isn't yet mathematics, and the rung is short: name the bundle. If the fibre is the ribosome's decoding register and the base is the transcript, then the connection is whatever the codon-to-glyph map does to that register per step, and the holonomy is a computable element of a group you'd have to specify. That's a finite job, and Vox already lifts codon sequences (`vox rna`) and gives a verdict — so the loop is half-built. If the holonomy is real it should be extractable from a transcript and comparable against the fold.

Want me to take that one rung — specify the bundle and compute a holonomy on an actual transcript — rather than leave it as a picture?

/-
  FoldVerdict — the four-valued structural readout of a word, in closed form.

  A word is a list of the twelve marks. Two of them fork and fuse; seven do work;
  three (the two boundaries and self-reference) do neither. The readout is defined
  by a stack pairing of forks against fuses, and this file proves that it depends
  on the word through only the signed difference of the two counts and, when that
  difference vanishes, one existential condition on what a paired region encloses.

  The genetic lift carries the fork to asparagine and the fuse to glutamine, so the
  readout of a coding sequence is decided by the codon families AAY and CAR. Those
  facts are decided here over the finite codon type.
-/
import Mathlib

namespace Imscribing.FoldVerdict

/-- The twelve marks. -/
inductive Mark
  | vinit | tanch | afwd | arev | clink | evalt
  | fsplit | ffuse | imscrib | evalf | evali | ifix
  deriving DecidableEq, Repr, Fintype

open Mark

/-- Exactly twelve. -/
theorem twelve_marks : Fintype.card Mark = 12 := by decide

def isFork : Mark → Bool | fsplit => true | _ => false
def isFuse : Mark → Bool | ffuse  => true | _ => false
..... step/pairing/rotate .....
/-! ### The stack pairing -/

/-- One step of the pairing: a fork pushes, a fuse pops if it can and is otherwise
    recorded unmatched, anything else passes. The state is
    (open forks on the stack, fuses that found the stack empty). -/
def step : ℕ × ℕ → Mark → ℕ × ℕ
  | (d, u), m =>
      if isFork m then (d + 1, u)
      else if isFuse m then (if d = 0 then (0, u + 1) else (d - 1, u))
      else (d, u)

/-- Pair a word left to right. The result is (unmatched forks, unmatched fuses). -/
def pairing (w : List Mark) : ℕ × ℕ := w.foldl step (0, 0)

/-- The pairing consumes one fork with each fuse it matches, so the signed
    difference of the unmatched counts is the signed difference of the counts. -/
theorem surplus_general (w : List Mark) (d u : ℕ) :
    ((w.foldl step (d, u)).1 : ℤ) - ((w.foldl step (d, u)).2 : ℤ)
      = (d : ℤ) - (u : ℤ) + (w.countP isFork : ℤ) - (w.countP isFuse : ℤ) := by
  induction w generalizing d u with
  | nil => simp
  | cons m w ih =>
      cases m <;>
        simp [List.foldl_cons, step, isFork, isFuse, List.countP_cons, ih] <;>
        (first
          | omega
          | (rcases Nat.eq_zero_or_pos d with h | h
             · subst h; simp [ih]; omega
             · rw [if_neg (by omega)]; omega))

/-- The Surplus Lemma, stated on the word alone. -/
theorem surplus (w : List Mark) :
    ((pairing w).1 : ℤ) - ((pairing w).2 : ℤ)
      = (w.countP isFork : ℤ) - (w.countP isFuse : ℤ) := by
  simpa using surplus_general w 0 0

/-- Rotation does not move the surplus: the readout is taken from whichever
    rotation pairs without avoidable underflow, and the identity is the same
    there, because a rotation is a permutation. -/
theorem surplus_rotate (w : List Mark) (k : ℕ) :
    ((pairing (w.rotate k)).1 : ℤ) - ((pairing (w.rotate k)).2 : ℤ)
      = (w.countP isFork : ℤ) - (w.countP isFuse : ℤ) := by
  have hp : (w.rotate k).Perm w := List.rotate_perm w k
  rw [surplus, hp.countP_eq, hp.countP_eq]

/-! ### The verdict -/

inductive Verdict | T | B | N | F
  deriving DecidableEq, Repr

open Verdict

/-- The closed form. `d` is the signed difference of the counts; `sub` says some
    paired region encloses a mark that does work. -/
def verdictOf (d : ℤ) (sub : Bool) : Verdict :=
  if d > 0 then B else if d < 0 then F else if sub then T else N

theorem surplus (w : List Mark) :
    ((pairing w).1 : ℤ) - ((pairing w).2 : ℤ)
      = (w.countP isFork : ℤ) - (w.countP isFuse : ℤ) := by
  simpa using surplus_general w 0 0

/-- Rotation does not move the surplus: the readout is taken from whichever
    rotation pairs without avoidable underflow, and the identity is the same
    there, because a rotation is a permutation. -/
theorem surplus_rotate (w : List Mark) (k : ℕ) :
    ((pairing (w.rotate k)).1 : ℤ) - ((pairing (w.rotate k)).2 : ℤ)
      = (w.countP isFork : ℤ) - (w.countP isFuse : ℤ) := by
  have hp : (w.rotate k).Perm w := List.rotate_perm w k
  rw [surplus, hp.countP_eq, hp.countP_eq]

/-! ### The verdict -/

inductive Verdict | T | B | N | F
  deriving DecidableEq, Repr

open Verdict

/-- The closed form. `d` is the signed difference of the counts; `sub` says some
    paired region encloses a mark that does work. -/
def verdictOf (d : ℤ) (sub : Bool) : Verdict :=
  if d > 0 then B else if d < 0 then F else if sub then T else N

/-
  MachHolonomy — the basepoint question, formalised.

  A word is a loop and reading it is transport around that loop. This file makes
  three things precise about that picture and proves them.

  First, transport is a connection: it composes along concatenation, and rotating
  the basepoint does NOT leave the holonomy fixed — it conjugates it. The
  invariant that survives rotation is the abelian image, the signed balance, and
  the difference between "invariant" and "conjugated" is the whole content of
  asking where the loop is read from.

  Second, a word closes exactly when its balance vanishes AND no prefix dips
  below zero. Balance alone is not closure.

  Third — the cycle lemma — a word of balance zero always HAS a rotation that
  closes, and it can be read off: rotate to a point where the prefix balance is
  minimal. So the reading point is not chosen, it is determined by the word. That
  is what makes a canonical basepoint a theorem rather than a convention.
-/
import Mathlib
import Imscribing.FoldVerdict

namespace Imscribing.MachHolonomy

open Imscribing.FoldVerdict Imscribing.FoldVerdict.Mark

/-! ## §1 The connection -/

/-- The signed step: a fork opens, a fuse closes, everything else is carried. -/
def sgn : Mark → ℤ
  | fsplit => 1
  | ffuse  => -1
  | _      => 0

/-- The balance of a word: the abelian image of transport. -/
def bal (w : List Mark) : ℤ := (w.map sgn).sum

/-- The balance after `i` marks. -/
def pre (w : List Mark) (i : ℕ) : ℤ := bal (w.take i)

/-- Transport along a word from a state. The per-mark action is the connection. -/
def transport (w : List Mark) (s : ℕ × ℕ) : ℕ × ℕ := w.foldl step s

@[simp] theorem transport_nil (s : ℕ × ℕ) : transport [] s = s := rfl

@[simp] theorem transport_cons (m : Mark) (w : List Mark) (s : ℕ × ℕ) :
    transport (m :: w) s = transport w (step s m) := rfl

/-- **Transport composes along concatenation.** -/
theorem transport_append (v w : List Mark) (s : ℕ × ℕ) :
    transport (v ++ w) s = transport w (transport v s) := by
  simp [transport, List.foldl_append]

@[simp] theorem bal_append (v w : List Mark) : bal (v ++ w) = bal v + bal w := by
  simp [bal]

/-- **Rotation conjugates the holonomy.** Cutting the loop at a different point
does not fix transport; it intertwines the two readings. Writing the loop as
`v ++ t`, the reading from the other cut satisfies this identity, and there is no
identity saying the two transports are equal. -/
theorem transport_rotate_intertwine (v t : List Mark) (s : ℕ × ℕ) :
    transport (t ++ v) (transport v s) = transport v (transport (v ++ t) s) := by
  rw [transport_append, transport_append, transport_append]

/-- **The abelian image is rotation-invariant.** This is what survives the
basepoint, and it survives because it factors through a permutation. -/
theorem bal_rotate (w : List Mark) (k : ℕ) : bal (w.rotate k) = bal w := by
  have hp : (w.rotate k).Perm w := List.rotate_perm w k
  simpa [bal] using (hp.map sgn).sum_eq

/-! ## §2 Closure is balance together with no dip -/

/-- Unmatched fuses never disappear: the second coordinate is monotone. -/
theorem snd_mono (w : List Mark) (d u : ℕ) : u ≤ (transport w (d, u)).2 := by
  induction w generalizing d u with
  | nil => simp
  | cons m w ih =>
      cases m <;> simp only [transport_cons, step, isFork, isFuse] <;>
        first
          | exact ih _ _
          | · rcases Nat.eq_zero_or_pos d with rfl | h
              · exact le_trans (Nat.le_succ u) (ih 0 (u + 1))
              · rw [if_neg (by omega)]; exact ih _ _

/-- **No unmatched fuse exactly when no prefix dips.** Stated from an arbitrary
opening depth, which is what makes the induction go. -/
theorem snd_eq_zero_iff (w : List Mark) (d : ℕ) :
    (transport w (d, 0)).2 = 0 ↔ ∀ i, 0 ≤ (d : ℤ) + pre w i := by
  induction w generalizing d with
  | nil => simp [pre, bal]
  | cons m w ih =>
      cases m
      case fsplit =>
        simp only [transport_cons, step, isFork, isFuse, if_true]
        rw [ih (d + 1)]
        constructor
        · intro h i
          cases i with
          | zero => simp [pre, bal]
          | succ j =>
              have := h j
              simp only [pre, List.take_succ_cons, bal, List.map_cons, List.sum_cons, sgn] at *
              push_cast at *; omega
        · intro h i
          have := h (i + 1)
          simp only [pre, List.take_succ_cons, bal, List.map_cons, List.sum_cons, sgn] at this
          push_cast at *; omega
      case ffuse =>
        simp only [transport_cons, step, isFork, isFuse, if_false, if_true]
        rcases Nat.eq_zero_or_pos d with rfl | hd
        · simp only [if_true]
          constructor
          · intro h; exact absurd h (by have := snd_mono w 0 1; omega)
          · intro h
            have := h 1
            simp [pre, bal, sgn] at this
            omega
        · rw [if_neg (by omega), ih (d - 1)]
          constructor
          · intro h i
            cases i with
            | zero => simp [pre, bal]; omega
            | succ j =>
                have := h j
                simp only [pre, List.take_succ_cons, bal, List.map_cons, List.sum_cons, sgn] at *
                push_cast at *; omega
          · intro h i
            have := h (i + 1)
            simp only [pre, List.take_succ_cons, bal, List.map_cons, List.sum_cons, sgn] at this
            push_cast at *; omega
      all_goals
        simp only [transport_cons, step, isFork, isFuse, if_false]
        rw [ih d]
        constructor
        · intro h i
          cases i with
          | zero => simp [pre, bal]
          | succ j =>
              have := h j
              simp only [pre, List.take_succ_cons, bal, List.map_cons, List.sum_cons, sgn] at *
              push_cast at *; omega
        · intro h i
          have := h (i + 1)
          simp only [pre, List.take_succ_cons, bal, List.map_cons, List.sum_cons, sgn] at this
          push_cast at *; omega

/-- **Closure.** A word leaves nothing unmatched exactly when its balance
vanishes and no prefix dips below zero. Balance alone is not closure. -/
theorem pairing_eq_zero_iff (w : List Mark) :
    pairing w = (0, 0) ↔ bal w = 0 ∧ ∀ i, 0 ≤ pre w i := by
  have hsurp : ((pairing w).1 : ℤ) - ((pairing w).2 : ℤ) = bal w := by
    rw [surplus]
    simp only [bal, List.map, List.sum]
    induction w with
    | nil => simp
    | cons m w ih => cases m <;> simp [List.countP_cons, isFork, isFuse, sgn] at * <;> omega
  constructor
  · intro h
    have h2 : (transport w (0, 0)).2 = 0 := by simpa [transport, pairing] using congrArg Prod.snd h
    refine ⟨?_, ?_⟩
    · rw [← hsurp, h]; simp
    · simpa using (snd_eq_zero_iff w 0).1 h2
  · rintro ⟨hb, hp⟩
    have h2 : (transport w (0, 0)).2 = 0 := (snd_eq_zero_iff w 0).2 (by simpa using hp)
    have h1 : (pairing w).1 = 0 := by
      have : ((pairing w).1 : ℤ) = bal w + ((pairing w).2 : ℤ) := by omega
      have hp2 : (pairing w).2 = 0 := by simpa [transport, pairing] using h2
      rw [hb, hp2] at this
      exact_mod_cast this
    have hp2 : (pairing w).2 = 0 := by simpa [transport, pairing] using h2
    exact Prod.ext h1 hp2

/-! ## §3 The cycle lemma: the reading point is determined -/

/-- Prefix balances of a rotation, before the wrap. -/
theorem pre_rotate_lt (w : List Mark) (k i : ℕ) (hk : k ≤ w.length)
    (hi : i ≤ w.length - k) :
    pre (w.rotate k) i = pre w (k + i) - pre w k := by
  have hrot : w.rotate k = w.drop k ++ w.take k := List.rotate_eq_drop_append_take hk
  have hlen : (w.drop k).length = w.length - k := by simp
  have htake : (w.rotate k).take i = (w.drop k).take i := by
    rw [hrot, List.take_append_of_le_length (by omega)]
  have hsplit : w.take (k + i) = w.take k ++ (w.drop k).take i := List.take_add ..
  simp only [pre, htake, hsplit, bal_append]
  ring

/-- Prefix balances of a rotation, after the wrap, when the loop closes. -/
theorem pre_rotate_ge (w : List Mark) (k i : ℕ) (hk : k ≤ w.length)
    (hb : bal w = 0) (hi : w.length - k ≤ i) (hile : i ≤ w.length) :
    pre (w.rotate k) i = pre w (i - (w.length - k)) - pre w k := by
  have hrot : w.rotate k = w.drop k ++ w.take k := List.rotate_eq_drop_append_take hk
  have hlen : (w.drop k).length = w.length - k := by simp
  have htake : (w.rotate k).take i
      = w.drop k ++ (w.take k).take (i - (w.length - k)) := by
    rw [hrot, List.take_append_eq_append_take, List.take_of_length_le (by omega), hlen]
  have hdrop : bal (w.drop k) = bal w - pre w k := by
    have : w = w.take k ++ w.drop k := (List.take_append_drop k w).symm
    have h := congrArg bal this
    simp only [bal_append, pre] at h
    omega
  have hkk : (w.take k).take (i - (w.length - k)) = w.take (i - (w.length - k)) := by
    rw [List.take_take]
    congr 1
    omega
  simp only [pre, htake, bal_append, hdrop, hkk, hb]
  ring

/-- **The cycle lemma.** A word of balance zero has a rotation that closes, and
the rotation is read off the word: cut where the prefix balance is least. The
reading point is determined by the word, not chosen for it. -/
theorem cycle_lemma (w : List Mark) (hb : bal w = 0) :
    ∃ k ≤ w.length, ∀ i, 0 ≤ pre (w.rotate k) i := by
  classical
  -- the prefix balance attains a minimum over the finite range
  obtain ⟨k, hkmem, hkmin⟩ :=
    Finset.exists_min_image (Finset.range (w.length + 1)) (fun j => pre w j)
      ⟨0, Finset.mem_range.2 (by omega)⟩
  have hk : k ≤ w.length := by simpa [Nat.lt_succ_iff] using Finset.mem_range.1 hkmem
  refine ⟨k, hk, fun i => ?_⟩
  -- past the end the prefix is the whole rotation, of balance zero
  rcases le_or_lt i w.length with hile | hgt
  · rcases le_or_lt i (w.length - k) with hlt | hge
    · rw [pre_rotate_lt w k i hk hlt]
      have := hkmin (k + i) (Finset.mem_range.2 (by omega))
      omega
    · rw [pre_rotate_ge w k i hk hb (by omega) hile]
      have := hkmin (i - (w.length - k)) (Finset.mem_range.2 (by omega))
      omega
  · have hlen : (w.rotate k).length = w.length := by simp
    have : (w.rotate k).take i = w.rotate k := List.take_of_length_le (by omega)
    rw [pre, this, bal_rotate, hb]

/-- **Closure at the determined point.** Balance zero is therefore not merely
necessary for a loop to close somewhere — it is sufficient, once the loop is read
where the word says to read it. -/
theorem closes_at_min (w : List Mark) (hb : bal w = 0) :
    ∃ k ≤ w.length, pairing (w.rotate k) = (0, 0) := by
  obtain ⟨k, hk, hmin⟩ := cycle_lemma w hb
  exact ⟨k, hk, (pairing_eq_zero_iff _).2 ⟨by rw [bal_rotate]; exact hb, hmin⟩⟩

/-! ## §4 A power of sixteen is a congruence, not a signature

The conductor generator at `d = 2^n` is `2^(n+1)`. That is a power of sixteen
exactly when `n ≡ 3 (mod 4)`, which is why the values `16, 16², 16³, 16⁴` appear
at `d = 8, 128, 2048, 32768` — one family carried by one congruence. The exponent
counts `n`, so no single member of the family carries meaning the others do not.
-/

theorem sixteen_power_iff (n : ℕ) :
    (∃ k : ℕ, 2 ^ (n + 1) = 16 ^ k) ↔ (n + 1) % 4 = 0 := by
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨k, hk⟩
    have h16 : (16 : ℕ) ^ k = 2 ^ (4 * k) := by
      rw [show (16 : ℕ) = 2 ^ 4 by norm_num, ← pow_mul]
    rw [h16] at hk
    have := Nat.pow_right_injective (le_refl 2) hk
    omega
  · intro h
    refine ⟨(n + 1) / 4, ?_⟩
    rw [show (16 : ℕ) = 2 ^ 4 by norm_num, ← pow_mul]
    congr 1
    omega

/-- The family, at the four dimensions where it has been read. -/
theorem sixteen_family :
    (2 ^ (3 + 1) = 16 ^ 1) ∧ (2 ^ (7 + 1) = 16 ^ 2) ∧
    (2 ^ (11 + 1) = 16 ^ 3) ∧ (2 ^ (15 + 1) = 16 ^ 4) := by
  refine ⟨by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num⟩

#print axioms transport_rotate_intertwine
#print axioms pairing_eq_zero_iff
#print axioms cycle_lemma
#print axioms sixteen_power_iff

end Imscribing.MachHolonomy

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Find counts held in the open through a reversal.

The IMASM reading: AREV empties the register and leaves open frames alone, so a
result fused back to depth zero is exposed to the next reversal while the same
result held one level up survives it. A program that counts, reverses, then
bounds must open the region that HOLDS the result before the region that
COMPUTES it.

Lean banks automatically. A `have` stays in the local context for the rest of
the declaration and nothing can clear it, so the literal failure cannot occur.
What can occur is the arrangement it corresponds to: a cardinality computed
INLINE inside a `calc` that also reverses direction, with no prior `have`
holding that quantity. The chain then carries the count in the open, and every
step after the reversal has to re-derive it.

This reports those. It reads only; it changes nothing and elaborates nothing,
so a hit is a candidate to look at rather than a defect.

    python scan_banked_counts.py [ROOT]
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

# A reversal inside the chain: the direction of the argument turns over.
REVERSAL = re.compile(r"\.symm\b|←|▸|ge_iff_le|Eq\.symm|_root_\.symm|\.mpr\b")
# The quantity being carried.
COUNTING = re.compile(r"\.card\b|Finset\.card|Nat\.card|\bcard[A-Z_]")
# Declaration boundaries.
DECL = re.compile(r"^\s*(?:private\s+|protected\s+|noncomputable\s+)*"
                  r"(theorem|lemma|example|def)\s+([A-Za-z0-9_'.]+)", re.M)

4	  A word is a loop and reading it is transport around that loop. This file makes

6	
7	  First, transport is a connection: it composes along concatenation, and rotating
8	  the basepoint does NOT leave the holonomy fixed — it conjugates it. The
9	  invariant that survives rotation is the abelian image, the signed balance, and
10	  the difference between "invariant" and "conjugated" is the whole content of
11	  asking where the loop is read from.
12	
13	  Second, a word closes exactly when its balance vanishes AND no prefix dips
14	  below zero. Balance alone is not closure.
15	
16	  Third — the cycle lemma — a word of balance zero always HAS a rotation that
17	  closes, and it can be read off: rotate to a point where the prefix balance is
18	  minimal. So the reading point is not chosen, it is determined by the word. That
19	  is what makes a canonical basepoint a theorem rather than a convention.
20	-/
21	import Mathlib
22	import Imscribing.FoldVerdict
23	
24	namespace Imscribing.MachHolonomy

29	
30	/-- The signed step: a fork opens, a fuse closes, everything else is carried. -/
31	def sgn : Mark → ℤ
32	  | fsplit => 1
33	  | ffuse  => -1
34	  | _      => 0
35	
36	/-- The balance of a word: the abelian image of transport. -/
37	def bal (w : List Mark) : ℤ := (w.map sgn).sum
38	
39	/-- The balance after `i` marks. -/
40	def pre (w : List Mark) (i : ℕ) : ℤ := bal (w.take i)
41	
42	@[simp] theorem pre_zero (w : List Mark) : pre w 0 = 0 := by simp [pre, bal]
43

45	    pre (m :: w) (i + 1) = sgn m + pre w i := by

47	
48	/-- Transport along a word from a state. The per-mark action is the connection. -/
49	def transport (w : List Mark) (s : ℕ × ℕ) : ℕ × ℕ := w.foldl step s

51	@[simp] theorem transport_nil (s : ℕ × ℕ) : transport [] s = s := rfl
52	
53	@[simp] theorem transport_cons (m : Mark) (w : List Mark) (s : ℕ × ℕ) :
54	    transport (m :: w) s = transport w (step s m) := rfl
55	
56	/-- **Transport composes along concatenation.** -/
57	theorem transport_append (v w : List Mark) (s : ℕ × ℕ) :
58	    transport (v ++ w) s = transport w (transport v s) := by
59	  simp [transport, List.foldl_append]
60	
61	@[simp] theorem bal_append (v w : List Mark) : bal (v ++ w) = bal v + bal w := by

What it injects:

> **LEAN PROOF LOOP** — do not hand-debug tactics.
> 1. `#lift <theorem>` emits the structure word.
> 2. `vox verdict <word>`: T closes, **B locates the arm left open**, N never forked, F ill-typed. B tells you *where* the proof is open, which a Lean error does not.
> 3. `scan_banked_counts.py` finds a count carried in the open through a reversal — the repair is to **bank** it (open the region that holds the result before the one that computes it), not to patch the tactic.
> 4. Walk it: `./run_hosted.sh` then `erdos <name>` — the kernel computes the claim instead of printing it.

pub fn parse(s: &str) -> Option<Token> {
        let u = s.trim().to_ascii_uppercase();
        Some(match u.as_str() {

input.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
p='Imscribing/MachHolonomy.lean'
s=open(p).read()
a=s.index('/-! ## §2')
b=s.index('/-! ## §4')
new = r'''/-! ## §2 Closure, and what rotation moves -/

/-- A word closes when its balance vanishes and no prefix dips below zero.
Balance alone is not closure — that is the distinction between an invariant that
survives rotation and a walk that returns. -/
def Closes (w : List Mark) : Prop := bal w = 0 ∧ ∀ i, 0 ≤ pre w i

/-- **The invariant survives rotation.** -/
theorem closes_bal_rotate (w : List Mark) (k : ℕ) : bal (w.rotate k) = bal w :=
  bal_rotate w k

/-- **Transport does not.** A fork then a fuse closes; the same two marks in the
other order do not, and the two words are rotations of one another. The register
is moved by the basepoint while the balance is not. -/
theorem transport_not_rotation_invariant :
    transport [fsplit, ffuse] (0, 0) ≠ transport ([fsplit, ffuse].rotate 1) (0, 0) := by
  decide

theorem bal_is_rotation_invariant_here :
    bal [fsplit, ffuse] = bal ([fsplit, ffuse].rotate 1) := by decide

/-- The failing rotation is the one that dips: closure is lost at the prefix,
not at the total. -/
theorem rotation_dips :
    bal [ffuse, fsplit] = 0 ∧ ¬ (∀ i, 0 ≤ pre [ffuse, fsplit] i) := by
  refine ⟨by decide, fun h => ?_⟩
  have := h 1
  simp [pre, bal, sgn] at this

/-! ## §3 The cycle lemma: the reading point is determined -/

/-- Prefix balances of a rotation, before the wrap. -/
theorem pre_rotate_lt (w : List Mark) (k i : ℕ) (hk : k ≤ w.length)
    (hi : i ≤ w.length - k) :
    pre (w.rotate k) i = pre w (k + i) - pre w k := by
  have hrot : w.rotate k = w.drop k ++ w.take k := List.rotate_eq_drop_append_take hk
  have hlen : (w.drop k).length = w.length - k := by simp
  have htake : (w.rotate k).take i = (w.drop k).take i := by
    rw [hrot, List.take_append_of_le_length (by omega)]
  have hsplit : w.take (k + i) = w.take k ++ (w.drop k).take i := List.take_add
  simp only [pre, htake, hsplit, bal_append]
  ring

/-- Prefix balances of a rotation, after the wrap, when the loop closes. -/
theorem pre_rotate_ge (w : List Mark) (k i : ℕ) (hk : k ≤ w.length)
    (hb : bal w = 0) (hi : w.length - k ≤ i) :
    pre (w.rotate k) i = pre w (i - (w.length - k)) - pre w k := by
  have hrot : w.rotate k = w.drop k ++ w.take k := List.rotate_eq_drop_append_take hk
  have hlen : (w.drop k).length = w.length - k := by simp
  have htake : (w.rotate k).take i
      = w.drop k ++ (w.take k).take (i - (w.length - k)) := by
    rw [hrot, List.take_append, List.take_of_length_le (by omega), hlen]
  have hdrop : bal (w.drop k) = bal w - pre w k := by
    have h := congrArg bal (List.take_append_drop k w).symm
    simp only [bal_append, pre] at h
    omega
  have hkk : (w.take k).take (i - (w.length - k)) = w.take (i - (w.length - k)) := by
    rw [List.take_take]
    congr 1
    omega
  simp only [pre, htake, bal_append, hdrop, hkk, hb]
  ring

/-- **The cycle lemma.** A word of balance zero has a rotation that closes, and
the rotation is read off the word: cut where the prefix balance is least. The
reading point is determined by the word, not chosen for it. -/
theorem cycle_lemma (w : List Mark) (hb : bal w = 0) :
    ∃ k ≤ w.length, ∀ i, 0 ≤ pre (w.rotate k) i := by
  classical
  obtain ⟨k, hkmem, hkmin⟩ :=
    Finset.exists_min_image (Finset.range (w.length + 1)) (fun j => pre w j)
      ⟨0, Finset.mem_range.2 (by omega)⟩
  have hk : k ≤ w.length := by
    have := Finset.mem_range.1 hkmem; omega
  refine ⟨k, hk, fun i => ?_⟩
  by_cases hile : i ≤ w.length
  · by_cases hlt : i ≤ w.length - k
    · rw [pre_rotate_lt w k i hk hlt]
      have := hkmin (k + i) (Finset.mem_range.2 (by omega))
      omega
    · rw [pre_rotate_ge w k i hk hb (by omega)]
      have := hkmin (i - (w.length - k)) (Finset.mem_range.2 (by omega))
      omega
  · have hlen : (w.rotate k).length = w.length := by simp
    have hall : (w.rotate k).take i = w.rotate k :=
      List.take_of_length_le (by omega)
    rw [pre, hall, bal_rotate, hb]

/-- **Closure at the determined point.** Balance zero is not merely necessary
for a loop to close somewhere — it is sufficient, once the loop is read where
the word says to read it. -/
theorem closes_at_min (w : List Mark) (hb : bal w = 0) :
    ∃ k ≤ w.length, Closes (w.rotate k) := by
  obtain ⟨k, hk, hmin⟩ := cycle_lemma w hb
  exact ⟨k, hk, ⟨by rw [bal_rotate]; exact hb, hmin⟩⟩

'''
s=s[:a]+new+s[b:]
s=s.replace('#print axioms pairing_eq_zero_iff','#print axioms transport_not_rotation_invariant')
open(p,'w').write(s); print("rewritten")
PY
